summary: Farm Studio is a mobile web app, in Arabic and English, that turns NASA Earth data into daily, field-level farm decisions in Jordan, presented as a simple farm game. A farmer draws their real field on a satellite map, and the app splits it into squares that follow its edges. It then reads NASA POWER climate records, SRTM elevation, and SMAP, MODIS and ECOSTRESS satellite data for that exact spot. With this it judges the crops the farmer wants to grow and builds a planting calendar from the local climate. It also turns a single weekly water allowance into a watering plan per crop: which days, how much, and whether the water is enough. Farmers log waterings by dragging a watering can over their field and get reminders on their phone. The app also marks safe spraying windows and warns ahead of frost, heat and heavy rain. This answers the Field Shift challenge by replacing fixed calendars and guesswork with climate-aware decisions grounded in open NASA data. It matters because Jordan is one of the world’s most water-scarce countries and its rainfall is falling, so every cubic metre and every season counts.
details:
What it does

Farm Studio helps farmers in Jordan make everyday decisions about water, crops, spraying and weather risk, using free NASA Earth observation data. It works on any phone, in Arabic or English, with no account needed.

  • Map your real field. The farmer finds their area by searching a town or village, or by using the shortcuts to farming regions from the Jordan Valley to Disi. They then tap the corners of their field on satellite imagery. The app shows each edge length and splits the field into squares of a size the farmer chooses, turned to follow the field's edges.
  • Check your crops. The farmer types the crops they want in their own words, for example "بندورة، عنب وزيتون" or "tomatoes and olives". Each crop is rated Useful, Can work or Not recommended, with the reasons: temperature, frost, winter chilling, water need, soil, crop rotation and the local climate trend.
  • Weekly watering plan. The farmer enters how much water they have per week. The app shares it between crops by need and says which days to water each crop and how much (mm and m³). It also says whether the water is enough or what share of the need it covers, and skips a watering when rain is coming. Farmers record real waterings by dragging a watering can over the squares, or by pressing and holding a square, and the plan updates from what they actually did.
  • Reminders. Reminders come on the watering day, the day before, and as a weekly plan for each crop, at times the farmer chooses. Each kind can be switched off. They appear in the app and can also arrive as phone notifications.
  • Crop calendar and harvest. Planting and harvest months are calculated from 25 years of local climate data. Ripe squares turn golden, and a sickle harvests them with a drag.
  • Safe-spray window. The next three days are colour-coded green, yellow or red using wind, gusts, rain, heat and humidity rules from pesticide labels. Red slots are locked.
  • Weather risks. Frost, heatwave, heavy-rain and strong-wind warnings come up to 7 days ahead, stronger for low-lying squares, with checklists of actions to take in the field.
  • Demo farm, farm key and export. A ready-made North Ghor farm is available for demonstrations. Farms are tied to the device, and a farm can be moved to another computer as a file.

How it works

  • NASA POWER (2001–2025 climatology, monthly series and daily observations) drives crop suitability, the planting calendar, the climate-trend advice, and vine harvest timing through growing degree days.
  • SRTM 30 m elevation finds low squares where cold air and water collect.
  • SMAP soil moisture, MODIS NDVI crop health and ECOSTRESS night-time surface temperature are fetched for each square through NASA AppEEARS.
  • Crop water use follows the UN FAO's standard method (FAO-56): a daily root-zone water balance for each square, using crop coefficients and reference evapotranspiration. Crop climate ranges follow FAO ECOCROP.
  • The 10-day forecast comes from Open-Meteo. If it is unavailable, the plan switches to NASA POWER data and is clearly marked as an estimate.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Less water wasted: water goes where and when the crops need it, and rain is used before pumped water.
  • Fewer losses from frost, heat, heavy rain and badly timed spraying.
  • Crop and calendar choices that fit a drying, warming climate. The North Ghor shows about −13% rainfall per decade in NASA POWER data.
  • Satellite data made usable for farmers and agricultural extension officers without technical training.

We plan pilots with farmers and the extension service of Jordan's Ministry of Agriculture, offline use, and calibration against local irrigation records.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy (SQLite), httpx, and cryptography for standard Web Push notifications.
  • Frontend: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, the Leaflet map library, an HTML canvas for the farm view, and a service worker for notifications.
  • Data: NASA POWER, AppEEARS (SMAP, MODIS, ECOSTRESS), SRTM via OpenTopography, Open-Meteo, ISRIC SoilGrids, OpenStreetMap, and Esri World Imagery.
  • Development: Git and GitHub, pytest (26 automated tests) and Playwright browser tests. It runs on any laptop or small server; no special hardware is needed.

What makes it creative

  • It turns scientific models into a familiar farm game: a fence around the farmer's real field, crops that grow and ripen, a watering can and a sickle to drag.
  • One workflow combines several NASA datasets for a single field, down to each square of it.
  • Farmers type crops in their own language and get plain-language reasons, not just scores.
  • A weekly water budget becomes a concrete schedule, plus reminders, for each crop.

What our team considered

  • Water scarcity: Jordan is among the most water-scarce countries in the world, so the weekly water budget sits at the centre of the app.
  • Real users: small farmers on phones, Arabic first, right-to-left layout, no sign-up, and simple gestures.
  • Trust: every number shows its data source, assumptions and limitations appear in the app, and nothing is invented. If a forecast is missing, the app says so instead of guessing.
  • Sustainability: it is built on free, open data with low running costs and modular code that is easy to maintain.
  • Limitations: crop parameters should be reviewed by an agricultural engineer for local varieties. The watering plan estimates soil water rather than measuring it, and SMAP satellite soil moisture is shown for comparison.
  • Use of AI: an AI coding assistant helped write code and text; the team reviewed and tested everything.
dataRefs: SMAP L4 Global 3-hourly 9 km Surface and Root Zone Soil Moisture (SPL4SMGP, version 8)
